The Village Genius

By: Kate Barry | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From Venda village to MIT marvel, meet the remarkable Mulalo Doyoyo: engineer, inventor, and award-winning researcher. He has now invented LICEM, a game-changing liquid cement that looks set to shake

Unique Selling Point:
Interview with Mulalo Doyoyo, as well as Roland Gustafson, former head of Volvo Concept Center and Chairman of the Next Generation Vehicles (NGV) initiative.
Demonstration of LICEM liquid cement strength test
Journey to Venda, Doyoyo's childhood home

Summary:
He grew up in Vondwe village with his grandparents and attended the local schools. A scholarship from the NG Kerk saw him sent to Mbilwi Secondary School – a school strong in science and mathematics - where he became Head Boy and matriculated in 1988.

With a bursary from Anglo American he attended the University of Cape Town, obtaining a BSc in Mechanical Engineering in 1993. He obtained his Honours degree in 1994 at Brown University in the USA, then two Master’s degrees: solid mechanics in 1995 and applied mathematics in 1996. In 1999 he defended his Doctoral thesis in Ballistics and went on to accept a post-doctoral research position at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). In 2004 he started lecturing at Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech).

He returned to South Africa in 2015 to contribute to the building of a democratic country and has lectured at UJ, and TUT. He founded an experimental laboratory for environmentally friendly chemicals and has come up with several inventions:

Ahifambeni: A hydrogen powered motorbike:

Amoriguard: Environmentally friendly paint https://amoriguard.co.za

Ecocast: Brick making machines that use less water and energy https://www.engineeringnews.co.za/article/locally-developed-low-water-brickmaking-machine-uses-industrial-waste-2016-07-08

Runza: A stainless steel motor vehicle suitable for SA’s terrain
https://www.news24.com/citypress/business/locally-manufactured-runza-car-comes-with-many-benefits-20200319

Cenocell: Cementless concrete https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenocell

Doyoyo says his inspiration for Cenocell came from his grandmother. She made pots from river clay, but with the addition of her ‘secret ingredient’ (frog urine) her pots were unbreakable. He found a substitute chemical that did the same job. His grandfather built stone structures which sparked his interest in structural engineering.

Further information:
Now the engineering world is excited by Doyoyo’s latest invention LICEM - a liquid cement that is an inexpensive, environmentally-friendly chemical concoction that does everything that cement does but a lot of things that cement does not do. It can activate fly ash to act like cement at a volume of 100%. It is inexpensive and environmentally friendly because the 9-chemical concoction includes several chemicals that absorb carbon dioxide, while beneficiating fly ash – a waste product from burning coal. These chemicals are manufactured in large quantities by many countries in the world including in South Africa. If Doyoyo’s innovation is adopted, the Portland cement industry will be as disrupted as fossil fuel vehicles will be by the production of electric vehicles. Doyoyo believes this is the solution to the scourge of cable and copper theft as well as potholes. LICEM concrete hardens fast and acquires high strength within an hour, to prevent criminlas from digging up underground cables. LICEM is cheaper, lighter, environmentally friendly but just as strong as traditional cement.

Extra Budget Items:
Return journey to Venda to visit Doyoyo's childhood home, his village schools, and traditional African environment - a far cry from the hallowed halls of Cambridge, MIT and Georgia Tech where he excelled.
Accommodation in Venda for one night.

THE VILLAGE GENIUS



Doyoyo: This is where I was born. This is where I have all the memories, I grew up here. It was a fun life. And we used to look after goats and cattle and sheep, everybody was happy.

V/O: This is Venda, the birthplace of Professor Mulalo Doyoyo, a mechanical engineer and inventor, whose most recent discovery may change the world. His roots remain deeply anchored in Venda culture and tradition.

As a boy he learned Tshikona, the traditional male dance performed at all important occasions.

Doyoyo: Tshikona dance, tshikombera, all those things, you know. I mean I’ve lived in so many big cities in the world, but when I see this, I feel very lucky to have been born here.

V/O: His brilliant career has taken him to the world’s foremost universities, but it all started at Vondwe Primary School.

Doyoyo: I was 6-years old when I started. We used to walk all the way from the riverside. The river is about 3 kilometres from here, so I used to come to those classes on top there. I just remember I didn’t have shoes like they have. You only wear shoes at Christmas time when your father comes back from Johannesburg.

V/O: But it was down at the river where he stumbled upon his grandmother’s secret that would later inspire his first major invention.

Doyoyo: She used to make clay pots like other old women, but in her case her pots were a lot stronger. So, when we were kids, we used to shoot them with like kettie, and then I would always be surprised. Why is my grandmother’s clay pots not breaking? Then I found something – her little secret.
You see how sticky it is? The frogs, when they do their business, they do it on this. So, it’s kind of like some organic chemical that they exude in their bodies, you know, and that chemical is basically this. That is one of my ingredients for cementless concrete, my invention in the USA, cementless concrete. It comes from this kind of stuff.

Fade to black

V/O: After water, cement is the most widely used substance on Earth. But the cement industry accounts for 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions, because the raw materials need to be heated to 1500 degrees. It contributes three times as much to global warming as the airline industry, bearing significant responsibility for the horrors of climate change.


Doyoyo: Portland cement, it’s made in an environmentally unfriendly manner by using coal. Now the challenge for the world is that, you know, they need to kind of limit its use.

V/O: And, like every other of his life’s challenges, it’s one that he’s embraced. In Grade 10 he outshone his peers and was sent to Mbilwi Secondary - a dedicated maths and science school.

Doyoyo’s accomplishments are still recorded in the principal’s yearbook from 1988.

Principal: Doyoyo, Reuben, with an A aggregate.

V/O: It was at this school that talent met opportunity.

Doyoyo: Anglo American had done an IQ test for us at the University of Venda. So, they automatically gave us scholarships. So, I chose to go to Cape Town.

V/O: After studying at UCT he was awarded a PhD from Brown University in the USA. He went on to lecture at one of America’s most prestigious colleges: Massachusetts Institute of Technology or MIT.

Doyoyo: At first, I was a little nervous that maybe for the first time I’m gonna fail the competition. But I did not lose. I had very good mentors. So, at MIT, I started working a lot with the car companies, the ultra-light consortium on automobile structures to create more fuel-efficient cars.

V/O: This is where he met Roland Gustaffson, a former Director of Volvo Technology Corporation.

Roland: I was, first of all, very impressed with his work at MIT and later on at the Georgia Tech.

Claire: Would you classify Professor Doyoyo as an exceptional scientist or engineer?

Roland: Both! Because I’ve been doing research for so many years, when I see excellence, I know it.

V/O: And his belief is justified, because Doyoyo’s latest invention – liquid cement - promises to be a game changer. It has zero carbon emissions, and uses fly ash, a toxic waste by-product that comes from burning coal to make electricity. Coal-fired power stations are surrounded by fly ash dumps.

Link: When you think of inventions that could potentially change the world that came out of a laboratory, we often have pre-conceived ideas of what that laboratory should look like. But even the greatest inventions can come from humble beginnings – like your townhouse balcony.

Prof: This is fly ash; this is sand, and this is stone. So, typically when you make concrete, this would be cement, it won’t be fly ash. So, what I have here is liquid cement, this is the invention. You can see it looks like water, I don’t usually pour a lot, you will see I don’t need a lot of water.

Claire: But I can see the viscosity is bigger than the water.

Prof: Yes, it looks kind of like gluey.

V/O: This concoction of 9 chemicals has the same binding capacity as powder cement but uses much less water.

Prof: In this process that you guys are seeing it absorbs carbon dioxide which is also another positive thing.

Claire: Wow!

V/O: Unlike powder cement, the chemical reaction is endothermic, meaning no heat is released.

Prof: You saw it’s a cold process, everything is at room temperature. This is more cost-effective, about a third of the cost of Portland cement.

V/O: And even though it’s a liquid, it’s as strong as Portland cement. We took samples to Sigmalab, a civil engineering materials testing laboratory in Centurion, run by Frank Grundling

Frank: The press will compress until the sample collapse, and we will record the kN, and from the kN we will do a quick calculation and determine what it the MPA?

Claire: What is that?

Frank: The strength of the concrete.

V/O: This particular sample reached 50.6 MPA’s before collapsing, that means a high-strength concrete.

Frank: This is a product that can be used in the construction industry, not only in concrete. We’ve done some testing on the soil, for soil stabilization in the roads, and we did find that the quality of the material did improve.

Claire: Professor Doyoyo’s liquid cement seems to have endless potential – versatile enough for simple applications like garden furniture and filling in potholes, and strong enough for big structures like bridges and water reservoirs.

Roland: Definitely, it’s a game changer because here you can use fly ash and some chemicals on site. I mean it’s a huge invention.

Doyoyo: So, there are trillions of tons of fly ash all over the world. Now the world is seeking to remove that fly ash from the environment. Now we have a technology that we can export to assist the world. It’s an opportunity for the country.
